reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an instructional tutorial on navigating eBay help topics and contacting support about listing-related questions. The phone number, one-time passcode, email form, and addresses are described as support-contact procedures, while no financial solicitation or deceptive outcome is demonstrated. The support identity and destinations may warrant external verification, but the described context is ordinary seller-support instruction.

If your answer is not shown there then click on contact us shown in blue color right under Need Assistance.

opening.argument: The presentation links access to seller assistance with concrete actions that can expose a viewer to verification or account-handling risk: it directs sellers into the support flow, asks them to use a phone number and one-time passcode, and presents separate email destinations for seller verification and logistics. The combination is more than generic business advice because the viewer is told to contact these destinations to resolve issues. The video does not independently establish that every displayed destination is an official, secure channel, so a purported support route could function as a low-barrier verification funnel.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The instructional framing does not resolve the central concern. The video specifically connects a support identity with contacting displayed destinations, including a seller-verification address, while the screen presents a phone number and one-time passcode. Calling this ordinary navigation assumes the support identity is authentic; the quoted procedures themselves do not prove that.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These details show a support workflow, not a promised reward or acquired asset. The screen labels the route as contact options and the email form asks for an item number and a question, while the description says the purpose is to get seller queries resolved. Nothing establishes payment, withdrawal, account takeover, or a deceptive outcome.

citations.quote: So in this tutorial I have shown how you can contact Ebay seller support and get your queries resolved.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together in a supposedly routine support tutorial: a phone contact option, a one-time passcode, an email form, and multiple direct addresses for seller verification and logistics. The caller is told that the passcode enables faster service, and the email instructions require login-related interaction and an item number. Those features create a verification-style path where viewers may disclose information or follow a destination they have not independently authenticated. The material therefore warrants scam treatment despite its calm tutorial tone.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The ordinary-looking interface is not dispositive. A polished support screen can still make a risky request appear routine, and the video amplifies the passcode and direct email routes rather than limiting viewers to a verified in-site channel. The presence of a tutorial format does not authenticate the destinations or explain why separate addresses should be trusted.

opening.argument: Although presented as education, the video actively promotes a set of contact routes. It tells viewers to select a support path, call or email, and separately supplies addresses for seller verification and logistics. The description also urges viewers to subscribe for more marketplace and ecommerce material. This makes the content a participation funnel: viewers are steered from a claimed eBay-support identity toward direct contact and further channel engagement, while the video provides no independent authentication of the destinations.

That steering matters because the asserted eBay-support identity is the basis for the requested participation, yet the opening does not establish that identity independently.
